title: Pay Transparency: What It Is, Benefits and Laws by State
summary: Pay transparency is gaining traction across the country. Learn what pay transparency is and what it means for your business.
body_markdown:
As employees and job candidates across the country expect greater clarity from organizations, certain states aim to require it for compensation. Ideally, pay transparency — or openly sharing salary data — may reduce pay inequity, wage discrimination and other potentially harmful practices.


On the other hand, businesses that have successfully grown and operate without pay transparency could be daunted by managing a new requirement. After all, no two states share identical laws. Between jurisdictions, an employer may need to disclose:


- entry-level pay
- [benefits](https://www.paycom.com/resources/webinars/unique-employee-benefits-what-does-your-workforce-really-want/)
- salary ranges
- individual salaries


Whether you face a new rule’s effective date or want to learn what salary transparency could do for your workforce, we’ll help you understand the concept and the differences between state requirements.


## What is pay transparency?


Pay transparency is the practice of openly sharing pay information with employees and potentially the public. While it could be limited to salaries, pay transparency also could apply to:


- bonuses
- stock options
- commission structures
- compensation increases associated with promotions
- wage ranges for specific roles and departments


A relatively new concept, no law outright prohibits a company from sharing this information. But in 2019,[Colorado](https://www.cnbc.com/2023/09/18/why-pay-transparency-is-on-the-rise-for-jobseekers.html) became the first state to require pay transparency (the law itself took effect in 2021).


## What are pay transparency laws?


Pay transparency laws refer to any active legislation that requires businesses to disclose compensation info. Some rules may only mandate internal transparency, while others require sharing this data with the public — primarily through job postings.


Simply the presence of pay transparency laws in a certain state doesn’t mean they cover every company. For example, New York’s[Fostering Access, Rights and Equity (FARE) grant](https://dol.ny.gov/pay-transparency-law-fare-grant) only applies to private employers with more than three workers. Hawaii’s[Act 203](https://labor.hawaii.gov/hcrc/files/2023/11/Act-203-Pay-Transparency-Equal-Pay.pdf) , on the other hand, doesn’t apply to organizations in the Aloha State with less than 50 employees.


Additionally, pay transparency laws can require businesses to make their workforce aware of potential promotions and advancement opportunities. Known as “[promotion transparency](https://news.bloomberglaw.com/esg/states-put-new-spin-on-pay-gap-laws-with-promotion-transparency-1) ,” legislation like the second part of Colorado’s[Equal Pay for Equal Work Act](https://cdle.colorado.gov/dlss/labor-laws-by-topic/equal-pay-for-equal-work-act) requires employers to notify *every* employee of advancement opportunities within the organization, regardless of department.


If salary transparency gains more momentum, we could see variations on these requirements or new concepts related to hiring and change management.


## Which states have pay transparency laws in 2026?


These 17 states currently require (or will require) pay transparency:


- California
- Colorado
- Connecticut (amendments go into effect Oct. 1, 2026)
- Delaware (law goes into effect Sept. 26, 2027)
- Hawaii
- Illinois
- Maine
- Maryland
- Massachusetts
- Minnesota
- Nevada
- New Jersey
- New York
- Rhode Island
- Vermont
- Virginia
- Washington


Salary transparency isn’t limited to how much employees get paid, either. Certain laws give candidates and current workers insight into what they *could* earn with the organization, too. For instance, a potential applicant might keep their options open if they clearly can see the salary ceiling for an employer.


While unique in individual guidance, these laws share common purposes to:


- enhance visibility
- reduce wage disparities
- boost financial well-being
- empower individuals to make more informed employment decisions


Whether salary transparency is ideal for your organization is beside the point. If where your company operates requires it, your compliance depends on understanding the concept and adhering to applicable state rules.


### *U.S. pay transparency laws by state*


Even if pay transparency laws don’t immediately affect your operations, it’s not a bad idea to proactively grasp them. Eventually, your state(s) or even a federal requirement could mandate the practice.


Keep the following states with pay transparency laws in mind as you adjust your compliance strategy.


#### California


The[California Equal Pay Act](https://www.dir.ca.gov/dlse/california_equal_pay_act.htm) went into effect in early 2023. While employers with one employee need to disclose salary ranges only upon their workers’ request, those with at least 15 employees — even with just one working in California — must:


- provide salary ranges for all job postings
- give employees a specific role’s salary range upon request
- *not* ask a job candidate about their pay history


Employers in California must also retain records of job descriptions and pay disclosures for both the duration of a worker’s employment *and* for at least three years after termination. Organizations that violate this law may face civil penalties of up to $10,000 per violation and employee lawsuits.


#### Colorado


Since Jan. 1, 2021, Colorado’s pay transparency law requires *all* employers with at least one worker in the state to announce promotion opportunities to every employee in Colorado the same day the position opens. With every job posting, employers also must disclose:


- hourly wages or salaries
- benefit information
- any other applicable compensation


Amendments from 2023 require that employers provide additional information if the position has a career progression. Employers must disclose and make available to all eligible employees requirements for career progression and when open applications are intended to be closed, in addition to each position’s terms of compensation, benefits, full-time or part-time status, duties and access to further advancement.


Employers that violate this law could face fines of up to $10,000 per violation and face employee lawsuits.


#### Connecticut


Connecticut’s Public Act 21-30 went into effect on Oct. 1, 2021. Similar to Colorado’s law, Connecticut employers must disclose pay data during the hiring process at the candidate’s request *or* prior to making a job offer.


Similarly, the state requires companies to disclose salary info to current local employees upon request or when they change positions.


Effective Oct. 1, 2026, House Bill 5003 reaffirms the state’s commitment to pay transparency by placing additional obligation on employers to disclose compensation and benefit information, prohibits retaliation and clarifies that the law applies to positions performed in Connecticut or positions performed outside of the state that report directly to a Connecticut supervisor.


Employers that violate this law could face civil lawsuits and be found liable for:


- compensatory damages
- attorney’s fees and costs
- other legal and equitable relief


#### **Delaware**


Starting Sept. 26, 2027, House Bill 105 will require employers with 26 or more employees in Delaware to disclose the minimum and maximum pay range for a position in a job posting on:


- any applicable pay scale
- a previously determined range for the position
- the actual range of others currently holding equivalent positions
- the budgeted amount for the position


This law affects internal *and* external job postings, and these pay ranges must be disclosed before any discussion or negotiations around compensation. Employers must also retain records of job descriptions for at least three years, including any relevant pay disclosures.


Employers who violate this law may be subject to civil penalties of up to $10,000.


#### Hawaii


Hawaii requires businesses with 50 or more employees to provide salary ranges or[hourly wage rates](https://www.paycom.com/resources/blog/minimum-wage-rate-by-state/) with *every* job posting.


Notably, this data must accurately reflect what an employer reasonably expects to pay for a role. For example, if a company posts a salary range of $50,000 to $200,000, the higher figure *can’t* be informed by an unrealistic commission expectation. Employers that violate this law may be required to hire, reinstate or promote employees (with or without backpay), among other remedies. Employers could also face civil lawsuits, including potential attorney fees and other court costs, in addition to the cost of a possible judgement ruled against them.


Hawaii’s pay transparency law doesn’t cover promotions, internal transfers or public employees whose salary is set by a[collective bargaining agreement](https://www.shrm.org/topics-tools/tools/hr-answers/collective-bargaining-agreement) .


#### Illinois


[Illinois House Bill 3129](https://www.ilga.gov/legislation/billstatus.asp?DocNum=3129&GAID=17&GA=103&DocTypeID=HB&LegID=148283&SessionID=112) amended the state’s[Equal Pay Act of 2003](https://labor.illinois.gov/faqs/equal-pay-faq.html) . The amendment went into effect on Jan. 1, 2025, and requires employers with at least 15 workers to provide a wage scale for *all* job postings. Employers must also post, announce or otherwise inform all current employees of opportunities for promotion no later than the same calendar day the employer posts the job internally. (This does not apply to positions that[the state exempts from competitive selection](https://cms.illinois.gov/) .)


Additionally, covered companies must also provide a general description of the benefits in their[total compensation statement](https://www.paycom.com/resources/blog/prove-their-worth-creating-and-using-a-total-compensation-statement/) , including:


- bonuses
- stock options
- other financial incentives


#### Maine


Maine LD 54/HP 18 took effect July 29, 2026, and requires certain disclosures and recordkeeping on the part of employers. Under the new law:


- Employers with 10 or more employees must include a pay range in job postings.


- A “range of pay” may be based on factors such as an established pay scale, previous ranges for the position, current employee pay for similar roles or a budgeted amount.
- Positions compensated solely by commission must instead clearly state that compensation is commission-based.


- Employers must provide the pay range for a position to an employee upon request.
- Employers are also required to maintain records of each employee’s position and pay history throughout employment and for three years after employment ends.
- Employers that violate this law may face civil fines of up to $500 per violation and employee lawsuits.


#### Maryland


Since late 2020, the[Maryland Equal Pay for Equal Work](https://www.dllr.state.md.us/labor/wages/equalpay.shtml) initiative has required every employer to provide applicants with a position’s wage scale upon request. Under this law, employers must:


- disclose the minimum and maximum salary (or hourly wage) and benefits for each internal or external position performed in the state
- provide pay information to an applicant before holding a discussion around pay if the public or internal posting didn’t already contain it


Employers must also maintain pay transparency compliance records for at least three years after a position is filled. Even if the position is never filled, employers must still retain these records for at least three years after the open job was posted. Organizations that violate this law could face civil fines of up to $600 per employee or applicant.


#### Massachusetts


The Frances Perkins Workplace Equity Act, an expansion of the Massachusetts Equal Pay Act, took effect Oct. 29, 2025. The amendment requires employers with 25 or more employees to disclose the pay range for all job postings.


The legislation also allows employees to demand the pay range for their *current* position. Employers must also provide the pay range of a position to an employee who is offered a promotion or transfer, as well as to any employees who are applying for it. Employers that fail to comply could receive a fine of up to $1,000.


#### Minnesota


Minnesota’s pay transparency law took effect on Jan. 1, 2025. It requires employers with 30 or more employees at one or more sites in Minnesota to disclose a “good faith estimate” of the starting salary range and a general description of the total compensation package, such as healthcare and retirement benefits, in all job postings. The pay range may not be open-ended. If the employer doesn’t plan to offer a pay range, they have to disclose a fixed pay rate.


The legislation does not apply to remote positions that may be performed outside the state of Minnesota. Employers that violate this law may face enforcement action from the Minnesota Department of Labor and Industry, as well as the state’s attorney general.


#### Nevada


Nevada’s pay transparency law,[Senate Bill 293](https://archive.leg.state.nv.us/Session/81st2021/Bills/SB/SB293_EN.pdf) , went into effect on Oct. 1, 2021. It requires *all* employers to provide candidates with salary info for any role the applicant interviewed for.


Plus, any current employees seeking a promotion or internal transfer are entitled to a new position’s salary data if they:


- applied
- interviewed
- received an offer for the role
- requested the salary data


Employers that violate this law may face civil fines of up to $5,000 per violation and employee lawsuits.


#### New Jersey


New Jersey’s Pay Transparency Act went into effect on June 1, 2025. The legislation impacts employers that have 10 or more employees over 20 calendar weeks and either conduct business in New Jersey, employ individuals within New Jersey or accept applications for employment from within the state. Under this law, all job postings must include the pay range, annual benefits and any other forms of compensation.


Employers that violate this law may face civil fines of up to $600 per violation.


#### New York


New York requires employers in the state with four or more workers to disclose salary ranges for all positions, including promotions and transfers. The same guidance applies to jobs that can be performed in New York *or* outside the state that report to a New York-based supervisor, office or worksite.


Employers that violate this law may face civil fines of up to $3,000 per violation.


#### Rhode Island


Since 2023, Rhode Island’s[Pay Equity Act](https://dlt.ri.gov/regulation-and-safety/labor-standards/pay-equity-act) has required companies with at least one employee to disclose salary ranges for:


- current positions (by request)
- applicants *before* discussing an offer
- employees at the time of hire or prior to moving to a new position


Employers that violate this law may face civil fines of up to $5,000 per violation.


#### Vermont


As of July 1, 2025, employers with five or more employees must disclose the hourly wage or range of compensation in job postings for positions that are either physically located in Vermont or report to an office or worksite that is physically located in Vermont.


Commission-based positions are exempt, but employers should state that the position is compensated based on commissions. For tipped positions, employers should disclose the hourly wage or wage range and state that the position is paid on a tipped basis.


Employers that violate this law may face civil fines of up to $10,000 per violation.


#### **Virginia**


House Bill 636 and Senate Bill 215 prohibit Virginia employers from seeking or relying on a prospective employee’s wage or salary history. Employers must also disclose a wage or salary range in every public and internal job posting, including postings for promotions and transfers. Under the law, employers:


- cannot ask candidates about wage or salary history
- cannot rely on salary history to evaluate applicants or set starting pay
- cannot retaliate against applicants or employees who decline to share pay history or who request a pay range
- must include a good-faith wage or salary range in every job posting


Employers that fail to comply with this law could face penalties of up to $1,000 for a first violation and up to $5,000 for subsequent violations. Affected individuals may bring a civil action within one year. For job-posting violations, employers have a 15-business-day cure period after written notice.


#### Washington


The[Revised Code of Washington 49.58.110](https://app.leg.wa.gov/RCW/default.aspx?cite=49.58.110) went into effect on Jan. 1, 2023. It requires employers with 15 or more employees and openings that could be filled by state residents to:


- include salary ranges and a general description of all the benefits or other compensation to be offered for all job postings
- disclose pay for internal job transfers and promotions at an employee’s request


Employers that violate this law may face fines of up to $1,000 per violation and employee lawsuits.


### *States with proposed pay transparency laws*


In addition to the 17 states with current or pending pay transparency laws, the following have proposed similar legislation:


- Alaska
- [Kentucky](https://apps.legislature.ky.gov/record/23rs/hb198.html)
- [Michigan](https://www.legislature.mi.gov/(S(hs1ybj3h55dwhaztzhiw3owa))/mileg.aspx?page=getObject&objectname=2023-HB-4406)
- Missouri
- Montana


Employers who operate in these jurisdictions should pay close attention to proposed pay transparency laws and similar regulations. Even if not passed, the legislation reflects an ongoing effort to introduce the concept — possibly where you operate.

## Five benefits of implementing pay transparency


Beyond compliance in states that require salary transparency, companies may experience several benefits from introducing the practice. Here are just five.


### *1. Promote employee trust*


Employees tend to trust organizations that value equity and fairness. Explaining how compensation is determined and distributed is one way of encouraging this. It could help your people feel more secure and comfortable in their current role if they have evidence of their competitive salary.


### *2. Support competitive pay structures*


Speaking of competitive pay, transparent compensation can prove to employees that they earn — or even exceed — the industry standard. This candor not only helps retention, but it also expands your team with top talent.


### *3. Drive employee productivity and engagement*


When employees know their pay sincerely reflects their roles and contributions, it’s easier to cultivate their commitment. After all, if you *knew* your pay was at the top of others with your career, would you feel compelled to work elsewhere?


### *4. Encourage pay equity*


Pay transparency can help diffuse bias and close the gap between gender, racial and other forms of wage disparities. Shining a light on these issues doesn’t mean your company is fundamentally flawed, but it *does* help identify areas where you could be more equitable.


### *5. Increase applicant interest*


Salary ranges in job postings could help your business attract truly interested and motivated candidates. This practice diffuses the mystery and can help hiring managers get ahead of:


- potentially awkward conversations
- subverted expectations
- lost applicants due to disagreements over pay


## Three challenges of implementing pay transparency


Pay transparency has benefits, true, but introducing it may pose several obstacles. Consider the following three hurdles before and during implementation.


### *1. Constant compensation flux to align with the market*


If you work in an industry with erratic pay, it’ll be difficult to keep your compensation competitive. While you should regularly evaluate *all* your business’s practices, constantly updating and changing pay quickly can drain resources without:


- a benchmark
- a solid core strategy
- an understanding of market trends


### *2. Employee discomfort with pay disclosure*


It’s useless to avoid the elephant in the room: If employees suddenly know each other’s pay, they may question why they get paid differently. With harsh enough disparities, pay transparency could create tension among your people.


On one hand, it could trigger certain employees to feel undervalued or underappreciated. Conversely, some workers may feel the need to hide or defend their wage. Addressing both groups could be difficult without a categorical — and likely costly — adjustment to your compensation strategy.


### *3. It doesn’t fully close wage gaps*


Pay transparency can help address inequity at work, but it’s not the sole fix. Cultivating equity requires addressing other issues, like:


- favoritism
- bias in hiring and promotions
- unequal access to development opportunities
- a toxic work culture


Your company may benefit from pay transparency, but no one concept truly can correct systemic issues. That takes time, dedication and a willingness to change as legal requirements and employee expectations demand it.


## How to stay compliant with pay transparency laws


Introducing pay transparency can be daunting — and necessary — if your state requires it. Even if it’s not mandated, the concept could help your organization foster a more equitable culture. Ultimately, that responsibility lies with the needs of your employees and executive leadership.


Keep in mind that, where required, pay transparency may be a vital part of your organization’s compliance requirements. When in doubt, consult with a licensed legal professional to help ensure your business complies with any pay transparency rules that affect where you operate.


And in states that require internal pay transparency, consider adopting a truly single software that automatically finds errors and guides employees to fix them *before* submission. Doing so doesn’t just help reduce errors but also empowers employees with in-depth visibility into how their pay is calculated.


Regardless of why your business introduces pay transparency, keep these eight tips in mind as you roll it out.


### *1. Research current pay transparency laws by work location*


Before you implement any program, verify which — if any — current pay transparency laws affect your operations. Compliance obligations will inform situations in which you *must* disclose compensation info.


### *2. Conduct market research on pay ranges for each position*


Even if you have a decent idea about a role’s salary range, *research it* . Look into similar businesses or industries to ensure you maintain competitive ranges for the roles in your organization. This helps you understand where your company stands — and if it needs to pivot.


### *3. Audit any existing pay transparency practices against your research*


Based on your findings, evaluate your current (or lack of) practices. In doing so, you’ll spot where you may need to adjust:


- salaries
- benefits
- bonus structures
- other forms of compensation


### *4. Develop a core strategy for salaries based on roles*


Once you understand *what* your employees’ wages should be,[create a strategy](https://www.paycom.com/resources/blog/choosing-the-right-pay-structure/) to help guide you. Define every piece of compensation for each role and account for those that don’t exist yet.


Economic uncertainty — such as from inflation — may compel you to change, but this strategy provides a solid foundation from which to move forward.


### *5. Include HR and management on the pay transparency team*


Your initiative shouldn’t be built by a single department. HR pros and[leaders](https://www.paycom.com/resources/4-reasons-leaders-fail-and-4-ways-to-avoid-it/) from across the company could provide valuable input to smooth the transition to pay transparency. They’ll also help effectively implement and construct the new pay policies.


And train managers on pay transparency requirements. After all, creating a safe and healthy environment often falls on supervisors. They should make it clear that employees who discuss their pay shouldn’t fear retaliation.


### *6. Plan the rollout of new pay structures with your team*


With policies drafted, collaborate with the team you formed to better steer implementation. Everyone involved with the process should have a clear understanding of:


- goals
- the timeline
- their responsibilities


### *7. Communicate the pay transparency program to employees*


After you’ve finalized your policies, it’s time to present them to employees. Be sure to express these rules clearly and make it easy for your people to access them. However you convey this info, make sure it reflects:


- a commitment to pay transparency
- why it exists
- the changes employees should expect


Sticking the landing with open and honest communication helps build trust with your workforce.


### *8. Track and adjust pay practices as needed*


Pay transparency is more than a box to check. Implementing it effectively requires maintenance and willingness to change.


Continue to monitor and adjust your policies based on shifts in:


- the legal landscape
- job market
- your organization


Flexibility helps ensure your pay transparency policies remain responsive, effective and compliant.

## Pay transparency: FAQ


### *Do pay transparency laws apply to remote employees?*


Often yes — certain laws apply based on where the employee could work or where the employer is located, so remote roles tied to covered jurisdictions may apply.


### *Does pay transparency require posting exact salaries or just ranges?*


Most laws require a good-faith and realistic salary range rather than an exact salary, reflecting what an employer expects to pay.


### *Are bonuses, commissions and equity required to be disclosed?*


In many jurisdictions, employers must disclose additional forms of compensation, such as bonuses, commissions or equity, if they are part of the posted job opening’s compensation package.


### *Do small businesses have to comply with pay transparency laws?*


It depends on the jurisdiction. Certain requirements apply only to employers above a certain employee threshold, while others cover nearly all employers regardless of size.


### *How do pay transparency laws impact independent contractors?*


Certain laws explicitly include independent contractors or freelance roles, requiring pay ranges to be disclosed when advertising those positions.


### *What penalties apply for violating pay transparency laws?*


Penalties can include fines, civil penalties, back pay exposure and sometimes private lawsuits, with higher penalties for repeated violations.


### *What documentation should employers keep to prove compliance?*


Employers should retain job postings, compensation ranges, pay-setting rationale and records showing how ranges were determined and applied, as certain states have strict recordkeeping requirements.


### *How does pay transparency affect employer branding and recruitment?*


Pay transparency can help improve trust, expand applicant pools and reduce tension in negotiations, making employers more attractive to candidates. However, pay transparency may not benefit every organization equally.


### *Can payroll and HR software help automate pay transparency compliance?*


Yes, modern HR and payroll software can centralize pay ranges, standardize job postings, track compliance and reduce the risk of errors. Keep in mind, payroll tech that communicates seamlessly with other HR tools makes it easier to approach compliance holistically, as all data that affects payroll automatically flows into the process — without any manual rekeying or interpretation from HR.
